page.title: Modeling SAP and Non-SAP Data at the Right Grain

content.title: Modeling SAP and Non-SAP Data at the Right Grain
content.subtitle: How to combine financial, billing and non-SAP data without duplicating records, losing document-level information or processing more data than necessary.
content.heading: Enterprise analytics design case

items: SAP + non-SAP data
Grain, keys and cardinality
Design reasoning case

content.title: Connecting the data is the easy part
content.subtitle: Financial data, billing data and a non-SAP source had to support analysis by month, customer, region, material and individual document.

content.text: The question is not how to connect SAP and non-SAP data. It is at what grain they should be combined.

items: The sources can have different granularities.
A financial document may reference a billing document.
Some business rules can only be calculated correctly at document level.
Joining too early can process far more records than necessary.
Aggregating too early can remove information that later calculations need.

content.text: Two opposite risks: joining too early and aggregating too early.

content.title: Establish the grain, the keys and the cardinality first
content.subtitle: Joins, unions and aggregations are implementation choices. The grain decides which of them is valid.

items.description: Define which levels of analysis are needed and which business rules exist, before looking at table structures.
Define what one row represents. Confirm which fields identify it and validate that definition with the business or data owner.
Identify the keys that connect the datasets, including the financial-to-billing reference, and check that they are complete, consistent and available at the grain where they will be used.
Profile the data: compare row counts with distinct key counts on each side and look for duplicates in keys expected to be unique.
The join is safe. Records are neither repeated nor lost.
Measures on the "one" side are repeated for every matching record.
items.impact: Header-level measures must not be carried through the join without an allocation rule.

items.description: The join multiplies records and inflates measures.
items.impact: Resolve it with a bridge or by reducing one side to the grain of the other.

items: The grain is a statement about the business event, not about the table. Two tables with the same key can still describe different events.

content.title: Choose the operation that matches the relationship
content.subtitle: Each operation answers a different question about how the datasets relate to each other.

items.title: Join
items.description: Combine datasets that describe the same business entity at a compatible grain and whose relationship has been verified.

items.title: Union
items.description: Stack datasets that have the same grain and the same measure semantics.

items.title: Enrichment
items.description: Add descriptive attributes through a lookup without changing the grain of the main dataset.

items.title: Aggregation
items.description: Reduce the grain to what the consumer needs, only after the rules that depend on the lower grain have been applied.

content.title: Trade-offs in these decisions
items: Join early
Process more records
Aggregate early
Lose document-level information
Document-level detail
Higher processing volume
Aggregated model
Simpler consumption

items.title: When the analysis needs only monthly data
items.description: If no rule depends on document-level information, each dataset can be aggregated to the common grain before they are combined.
items.impact: Simpler model and lower processing volume.

items.title: When a rule needs document-level data
items.description: The detail must be preserved up to the point where the rule is calculated. Aggregation happens after that.
items.impact: Correct results at every level of analysis.

content.text: Aggregate as early as the rules allow, and no earlier.

content.title: Calculate each rule where it is correct, aggregate afterward
content.subtitle: A business rule that requires document-level data is calculated at document level. The final reporting layer can still be aggregated.

items.title: Source-aligned datasets
items.description: Each source is kept at its native grain with its keys. Only filtering and projection are applied.

items.title: Document-level integration
items.description: Financial and billing data are combined through the document reference. Non-SAP data is joined at the level of its own key. Document-level rules are calculated here, once.

items.title: Aggregated analytical layer
items.description: Results are aggregated to month, customer, region and material. Additive measures are summed; ratios are rebuilt from their components.

items.title: Consumption
items.description: Reports read the aggregated layer and stay simple. Document-level inspection is a drill-through to the integration layer.

content.text: Calculate at the grain where the rule is valid. Report at the grain the business needs.

content.title: Preventing duplicated records and incorrect measures
content.subtitle: Correctness comes before performance. A fast model that duplicates records is not an optimized model.

items: Declare the grain of every dataset and layer explicitly.
Verify key uniqueness on the side of each join expected to be unique.
Compare record counts before and after every join.
Reconcile totals between the source, the document-level layer and the aggregated layer.
Do not carry header-level measures through a 1:N join without an allocation rule.
Treat ratios and other non-additive measures separately from additive ones.

performance.title: How the performance implications are evaluated

items: Number of records processed at each step.
Where the data volume is reduced, and whether it is reduced before the expensive joins.
Cardinality of each join.
Which results are reused often enough to justify persisting them.
The effort required to maintain the model as new requirements are added.

content.title: The deeper lesson
content.subtitle: The key architectural question is not how to connect the data, but where each business rule should be applied.

items: Establish the grain before choosing a join, a union or an aggregation.
Verify keys and cardinality instead of assuming them.
Decide per business rule and per level of analysis, not globally.
Calculate once at the grain where the rule is valid, then aggregate for consumption.

The reasoning is independent of the platform. It applies in SAP BW, SAP HANA, SAP Datasphere or a lakehouse: determine at what grain datasets are combined, where each rule belongs and what can be reused.

content.text: Grain decides where each rule can live.
